factual_issues.claim: ReSeed's project computer: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, 96 CPU cores, 866 GB RAM, 4 × NVIDIA A100 80 GB.
factual_issues.problem: E does not document this hardware or operating system. The repeated claims that this is ReSeed's real computer therefore lack support.
factual_issues.evidence: E says only: “Retrain ForestNet (about 12 minutes on one GPU)”. It supplies no computer specification.
factual_issues.fix: Example workshop computer: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, 96 CPU cores, 866 GB RAM, 4 × NVIDIA A100 80 GB.

factual_issues.claim: These games were built on this very computer.
factual_issues.problem: E does not identify the computer used to create these games.
factual_issues.evidence: E documents website publishing as “GitHub Pages serves `site/` as committed, no build step”, but does not document the games' development machine.
factual_issues.fix: Case closed! Psst: now you can read a computer's spec sheet like a pro.

factual_issues.claim: The README reports 99.1% accuracy on satellite tiles.
factual_issues.problem: The supplied README gives no accuracy percentage. A precise score also needs a named evaluation set to make its meaning clear.
factual_issues.evidence: E says: “It is strong on satellite tiles and ground photos, weaker on unusual pictures”.
factual_issues.fix: Strong on satellite tiles; can still make mistakes (README)

factual_issues.where: GPU batch: 512 pictures at a time (train.py)
factual_issues.claim: ReSeed's training code uses batches of 512 pictures.
factual_issues.problem: E does not include train.py or specify a batch size, so this code-attributed number is unsupported.
factual_issues.evidence: E shows “python -m reseed.classify.train” with dataset and output arguments, but no batch-size setting.
factual_issues.fix: GPU batch: a group of pictures to learn from together

general_cs_errors.where: motherboard / text; Beep! Your computer passed its
general_cs_errors.claim: Every part plugs into the motherboard, and POST checks them all and proves every part is correctly placed.
general_cs_errors.problem: Some parts connect through cables or attach elsewhere. POST checks basic startup hardware; passing it does not certify every component or connection.
general_cs_errors.fix: The **motherboard** is the big board that links computer parts. The **PSU** supplies power. At switch-on, a quick self-test (**POST**) checks the basics—not every part.

general_cs_errors.claim: GPU helpers cannot make choices and only repeat one simple job.
general_cs_errors.problem: GPUs can execute conditional instructions. Similar work across many items is a strength, not their only capability.
general_cs_errors.fix: The helpers can make choices, but matching jobs help them work fastest.

general_cs_errors.where: The chef could, but one at a time
general_cs_errors.claim: The CPU can only process the work one item at a time.
general_cs_errors.problem: CPUs can work in parallel using multiple cores and vector instructions. This unqualified explanation contradicts the game's own multiple-chef analogy.
general_cs_errors.fix: The chefs can share the work too, but the helpers shine at lots of matching math!

general_cs_errors.where: Color 2 million pixels at the same time
general_cs_errors.claim: A GPU colors two million pixels simultaneously.
general_cs_errors.problem: GPUs process large images in many groups of operations, not necessarily all pixels at literally the same instant.
general_cs_errors.fix: Color 2 million pixels in speedy groups

hard_for_8yo.text: A **spec sheet** lists a computer's parts and sizes. **4 × 80 GB** means four GPUs with 80 GB each: 320 GB in total.
hard_for_8yo.simpler: A **spec sheet** lists computer parts. **GB** measures memory space. For GPUs, **4 × 80 GB** means four with 80 GB each: 320 GB total.

verdict: The kitchen analogy is engaging and mostly sound, but unsupported real-computer claims and a few absolute statements about hardware should be corrected before release.
